common_name: Vi Luihn Siberian Iris (Morgan Award Deep Violet Iris with Pale Yellow Signal)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Vi Luihn was bred by Sydney DuBose and introduced by Melrose Gardens, later winning the American Iris Society's Morgan Award.

directions: Vi Luihn carries deep violet-blue self flowers faintly netted with paler bee-guide veining around a small pale yellow signal, held on tall stems above narrow, grass-like clumps of foliage in midseason to late bloom. Like other Siberian iris, it tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and resists rot and borer problems, making it a durable choice near a pond edge or in a mixed border. Clumps can go many years without needing division; when they become crowded, dig and divide in early fall or right after spring bloom.

common_name: Coronation Anthem Siberian Iris (Morgan-Wood Medal Blue Bitone with Cream Center)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Coronation Anthem was bred by Robert Hollingworth and later won the American Iris Society's Morgan-Wood Medal.

directions: Coronation Anthem bears medium blue standards over deep blue, ruffled falls with a creamy white center surrounding a pale yellow blotch, held on a single bloom per stem above thin, grass-like foliage that stays attractive through summer. It tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and is far less prone to rot and borer problems. Clumps can go many years without needing division; when crowded, dig and divide in early fall or right after spring bloom.

common_name: Blueberry Fair Siberian Iris (Morgan-Wood Medal Ruffled Royal Blue Tetraploid Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; a tetraploid cultivar bred by Robert Hollingworth, later winning the American Iris Society's Morgan-Wood Medal.

directions: Blueberry Fair produces broad-petaled, heavily ruffled royal-blue to violet-blue flowers with a white signal, a hallmark of the tetraploid Siberian iris from Hollingworth's breeding program, above narrow, grass-like clumps of foliage in midseason. It tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and resists rot and borer problems. Clumps can go many years without division; when crowded, dig and divide in early fall or right after spring bloom.

common_name: Fond Kiss Siberian Iris (Morgan-Wood Medal Ivory White Iris with Pink-Flushed Falls)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Fond Kiss was bred by Marty Schafer and Jan Sacks, later winning the American Iris Society's Morgan-Wood Medal.

directions: Fond Kiss opens ivory-white flowers with broad, waved standards and broad falls carrying a delicate pink-lavender flush at the base and fine veining at the throat; three buds open in slow succession in late spring to early summer above narrow, grass-like foliage. It tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and resists rot and borer problems. Clumps can go many years without division; when crowded, dig and divide in early fall or right after spring bloom.

common_name: Riverdance Siberian Iris (Morgan-Wood Medal Cornflower Blue Ruffled Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Riverdance was bred by Marty Schafer and Jan Sacks, later winning the American Iris Society's Morgan-Wood Medal.

directions: Riverdance bears large, rolling-ruffled cornflower-blue flowers, with falls flecked white at the shoulders and edged in a fine white wire rim around a yellow-centered white signal, held on tall stems above narrow, grass-like clumps of foliage. It tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and resists rot and borer problems. Clumps can go many years without division; when crowded, dig and divide in early fall or right after spring bloom.

common_name: Miss Apple Siberian Iris (Peacock Butterfly Series Red-Violet Iris with Yellow Signal)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Miss Apple is part of the Peacock Butterfly series bred by Marty Schafer and Jan Sacks and won the American Iris Society's Morgan-Wood Medal.

directions: Miss Apple carries lightly fragrant, richly colored flowers with lighter violet-pink to magenta standards over deep, mulberry-red falls blended with yellow and centered on a showy warm-yellow signal, among the truest reds yet bred into Siberian iris, held on slender stems above sword-shaped, grass-like foliage. It tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and resists rot and borer problems. Clumps can go many years without division; when crowded, dig and divide in early fall or right after spring bloom.

common_name: Son of Sun Spuria Iris (Nies Medal Bright Yellow Spuria Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall so roots establish before winter; Son of Sun won the President's Cup at an American Iris Society Convention and later the Nies Medal.

directions: Set rhizomes shallowly, just below the soil surface, in rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Son of Sun carries lightly ruffled, clear bright yellow self flowers of excellent form on tall, sturdy stems above sword-like foliage in midseason, and its clean color and vigorous habit made it one of the most widely honored spurias of its era. Water generously from fall through the spring bloom period, then withhold water during the plant's summer dormancy to prevent rot. Feed generously in early spring and leave clumps undisturbed for several years, since spurias resent frequent digging and rebloom slowly after division.

common_name: Cinnamon Stick Spuria Iris (Nies Medal Maroon-Brown Iris Speckled with Gold)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall so roots establish before winter; Cinnamon Stick was bred by O. David Niswonger and won the American Iris Society's Nies Medal, later serving as a parent of the Nies Medal winner 'Sultan's Sash'.

directions: Cinnamon Stick bears maroon-brown standards over a maroon ground on the falls that is heavily speckled with gold, an unusual warm-toned break from the yellow and blue shades typical of spurias, on tall stems above sword-like foliage in midseason. Water generously from fall through spring bloom, then withhold water during summer dormancy to prevent rot. Feed generously in early spring and leave clumps undisturbed for several years, since spurias resent frequent digging and rebloom slowly after division.

common_name: Adriatic Blue Spuria Iris (Nies Medal Deep Blue Iris with Gold-and-Blue Falls)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall so roots establish before winter; Adriatic Blue was awarded Honorable Mention, then Award of Merit, and later the American Iris Society's Nies Medal.

directions: Adriatic Blue carries deep blue standards and style arms over falls of gold rimmed in deep blue, a striking bicolor break among Nies Medal spurias, on tall stems above sword-like foliage in midseason. Water generously from fall through spring bloom, then withhold water during summer dormancy to prevent rot. Feed generously in early spring and leave clumps undisturbed for several years, since spurias resent frequent digging and rebloom slowly after division.

planting.note: Divide and transplant rhizome clumps in fall as rains return, setting the fans shallowly in fast-draining, slightly acidic soil with the crown at or just above grade; the Jepson eFlora treats Thompson's Iris as a distinct species, though some other floras have historically classified it as a natural hybrid between Iris innominata and Iris douglasiana.

directions: Thompson's Iris is a Pacific Coast iris restricted to the lower Klamath Range of Del Norte County, California, and adjacent southwestern Oregon, where it grows on sunny, lightly wooded slopes with dark green, ribbed, evergreen foliage that is red-tinged at the base. In spring it sends up pale to deep blue-violet flowers, occasionally white or gray, distinguishing it in the field from the golden-flowered Iris innominata it grows alongside and with which it was long lumped taxonomically. It tolerates summer drought once established and resents disturbance, so division should be done sparingly.
sources: Society for Pacific Coast Native Iris (SPCNI)

common_name: Canyon Snow Douglas Iris (White Pacific Coast Iris with Golden Blotch)

planting.note: Divide and transplant rhizome clumps in fall as rains return, setting the fans shallowly in fast-draining, slightly acidic soil with the crown at or just above grade; Canyon Snow was selected from Iris douglasiana 'Alba' seedlings by a California horticulturist and introduced by a botanic garden.

directions: Canyon Snow produces large white flowers with a bright golden-yellow blotch at the base of each fall, held over glossy, evergreen, grass-like foliage that slowly spreads into wide clumps. Since its introduction it has become one of the most widely planted Pacific Coast iris selections, valued for disease resistance, vigorous growth, and a long spring bloom season. It tolerates summer drought once established and resents disturbance, so division should be done sparingly, only every several years.

common_name: Canyon Sunshine Pacific Coast Hybrid Iris (Butter-Yellow Iris with Lemon Center)

planting.note: Divide and transplant rhizome clumps in fall as rains return, setting the fans shallowly in fast-draining, slightly acidic soil with the crown at or just above grade; Canyon Sunshine arose from a cross involving the Pacific Coast iris selection Canyon Snow and is grown as a garden hybrid rather than a wild species.

directions: Canyon Sunshine bears butter-yellow flowers with a lemony center over evergreen, grass-like foliage that spreads by rhizomes into wide clumps. It tolerates full sun on the coast but appreciates afternoon shade inland, and it makes a good drought-tolerant, deer-resistant planting for the understory of oaks once established. As with other Pacific Coast iris hybrids, it resents disturbance, so division should be done sparingly.

common_name: Mission Santa Cruz Pacific Coast Hybrid Iris (Rose-Magenta Self)
scientific_name: Iris Pacific Coast Hybrid 'Mission Santa Cruz'

planting.note: Divide and transplant rhizome clumps in fall as rains return, setting the fans shallowly in fast-draining, slightly acidic soil with the crown at or just above grade; Mission Santa Cruz was bred by Joseph Ghio and introduced by Bay View Gardens.

directions: Mission Santa Cruz is a compact Pacific Coast iris hybrid with glowing rose-red to magenta self-colored flowers on short stems above evergreen, grass-like foliage in midseason. It tolerates summer drought once established and, like other Pacific Coast iris hybrids, resents disturbance, so division should be done sparingly and clumps left undisturbed for several years to build up bloom.
